# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Ada | 1 |
| Second | Bo | 2 |
| Third | Cora | 3 |
| Fourth | Dev | 4 |
| Fifth | Emi | 5 |
| Sixth | Finn | 6 |
| Seventh | Gia | 7 |
| Eighth | Hal | 8 |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

[Competition deals](competition-deals.md) covers board identity. [Competition ties](competition-ties.md) covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.

# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in [competition pairing](competition-pairing.md), and the dimensions of the playing board are in [competition boards](competition-boards.md).

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md). This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.

# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper | Meaning at this boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)` | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively |
| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)` | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete validation sequence; [Snapshot selection notes](snapshot-selection-notes.md) explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Action timestamps may be much larger than the elapsed clock cap. The replay evaluator advances the logical timeline using safe integers, while `advanceGame` caps the resulting elapsed counter. That distinction prevents a legitimate long timeline from being rejected merely because the visible clock has saturated. [Replay format](replay-format.md) explains exact timeout edges and equal-time order.

## Failure reports that preserve the evidence

For current snapshot failures the decoder deliberately supplies no reason. The most effective local investigation isolates a single change against a known accepted object: replace just the selection, just the code, or just one counter. The tests in `snapshot.test.ts` use this pattern so that an unrelated invalid baseline cannot hide a missing check.

Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.

Retaining original text matters when a failure depends on bytes or syntax. Parsing and reserializing a padded document can remove the very length excess that caused its rejection. A screenshot of a notice cannot establish whether an extra property was nested or at the root. For the current accepted shapes, use [Board code format](board-code-format.md), [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](replay-format.md); for the browser steps around them, use [Sharing FAQ](sharing-faq.md).

# Text entry policy

This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.

Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.

## One name representation

A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.

The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.

For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.

## Examples of representation

The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.

| Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
| `Ada   Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space |
| `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary |
| `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available |
| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |

The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.

NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.

A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.

## Drafts and accepted values

A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active.

That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.

The current Reproduction component provides a useful example of draft ownership, though its data is not a name. Its snapshot string lives in local React state and is sent to the decoder on Load snapshot. BoardCodeForm instead reads its native form field at submission. Either storage approach can host an input boundary; the choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.

No name persistence shape exists in `session/storage.ts`. Its preferences concern size and best move counts. Those fields contain no name preference key, snapshot property or import format.

## Board codes follow a different path

The Board code input is a native text input with `maxLength={32}`, spell checking disabled and autocomplete off. On submission, `use-game.ts` calls `code.trim()` before `parseBoardCode(code)`. That is the only cleanup in that loading path.

The grammar is a version prefix, supported side length and seed separated by hyphens. For example, surrounding spaces around `np1-6-1` are accepted by the control, but an internal space changes the grammar and is rejected. The loader does not collapse arbitrary interior text or repair the seed.

Successful submission replaces the game and refreshes the field from the current code because the input is keyed by generation. Unsuccessful submission preserves the draft. This gives a concrete reference for separating a draft from an accepted representation without applying name transformations to a deal identifier. See [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

Board-code parsing is also available as a core function. Calling `parseBoardCode` directly is not the same as passing through the UI loader's trim step. When reading a failure report, the entry point matters. A format parser and an input adapter can have distinct responsibilities without the application guessing what malformed identifiers meant.

## Snapshot text remains structured data

Snapshot JSON has a native textarea length limit and a decoder byte limit. It can include whitespace for readability, and export deliberately produces multiple lines. Its structure is validated before the game is replaced.

Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.

The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.

[Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) explain the current parser and feedback boundaries. Keeping those links close to the input descriptions is more useful than inventing one universal cleanup function for every field on the page.

## Unicode review considerations

Canonical equivalence is easiest to miss when examples are written as visually identical letters. A composed accented character and a base character followed by a combining mark may render alike while having different underlying sequences. A useful representation check includes both forms and inspects the accepted value rather than only its screenshot.

The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.

Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) provides the visual context.

The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.

## Implementation evidence to look for

There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.

Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.

The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries.

# Name length policy

This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.

The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.

## The checked value

The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.

The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.

A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.

## Code points, code units and visible text

JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.

A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form.

The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted.

In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.

## Boundary examples

The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist.

| Value | Code-point count | Length result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty string | 0 | Fails |
| `A` | 1 | Fails |
| `Al` | 2 | Passes |
| `A😀` | 2 | Passes |
| Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes |
| Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails |
| Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes |

The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing.

“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.

## The order is observable

A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.

A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.

There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.

## Scope of current evidence

There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.

When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.

# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.

For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.

# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.

# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The [game specification](../README.md) connects this stack to the other requirements.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
